entries.sentence: There is currently no cure for HIV.
It can be treated with antiretroviral medicines, and WHO describes it as a manageable long-term condition when prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care are available.
The virus stays in the body for life, but treatment keeps it under control and allows people to stay well.
People diagnosed with HIV in England receive treatment free of charge.
Some people have a short flu-like illness around 2 to 6 weeks after acquiring HIV, according to the NHS.
It can include a sore throat, a high temperature, swollen glands, muscle aches, tiredness and a skin rash.
The CDC says this illness may last a few weeks.
Other people have no symptoms in the first few weeks after infection.
After this early phase, HIV may cause no symptoms for many years, although the NHS says the virus keeps damaging the immune system during that time.
This is one reason an early diagnosis matters: treatment can then start sooner, which can improve the chances of controlling the virus.
When the immune system is weakened, infections can happen more often or be more severe.
WHO says HIV makes it easier to become ill with tuberculosis, other infections and some cancers.
HIV is passed on when infected body fluids get into another person's bloodstream, the NHS says.
WHO lists blood, breast milk, semen and vaginal fluids as the fluids involved.
The CDC explains that these fluids must reach a mucous membrane or damaged tissue, or be injected directly into the bloodstream.
The NHS adds that HIV can be spread by sharing needles.
It can also pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy and delivery and through breastfeeding, and effective treatment lowers the chance of this.
HIV does not spread through the air like cold and flu viruses, the NHS says.
WHO states that casual contact such as kissing or sharing food does not spread it, and the NHS describes passing it on through kissing alone as extremely rare.
MedlinePlus notes that risk is shaped by more than individual behaviour, since stigma, discrimination, income, education and where a person lives can all play a part.
The CDC adds that stigma and mistrust of health care may stop some people who inject drugs from seeking testing, care and treatment.
HIV is diagnosed with a test, and the NHS provides testing free of charge to anyone.
Options include testing at a sexual health clinic, a home testing kit and a home sampling kit.
With a home testing kit a person collects a saliva sample or a small spot of blood and tests it themselves, whereas with a home sampling kit the sample is posted to a laboratory.
A clinic may offer a finger-prick test with results in minutes, while a more detailed test can take a few days.
If a first test suggests HIV, a further blood test is needed to confirm the result.
A test may not detect HIV acquired very recently, a gap known as the window period, and its length differs between tests.
It is still possible to pass on HIV during the window period.
The CDC advises anyone who is pregnant to be tested as soon as possible, so that passing HIV to the baby can be prevented.
HIV is treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from replicating in the body.
These are taken every day as the doctor recommends, and the aim is an undetectable viral load.
NHS 111 Wales says most people taking daily treatment reach an undetectable viral load within about six months, and Terrence Higgins Trust says it can take up to six months for some.
Terrence Higgins Trust says treatment is recommended straight away and still protects the immune system when it has already been damaged.
Treatment is free on the NHS, regardless of immigration status according to the Trust.

Terrence Higgins Trust says someone on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass on HIV, and WHO says a person on treatment who is virally suppressed will not pass HIV to sexual partners.
This is often shortened to U=U, meaning undetectable equals untransmittable.
The Trust adds that a current sexually transmitted infection does not change this.
Condoms still help protect against other sexually transmitted infections and act as contraception.
The NHS says condoms are the most effective protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.
It advises water-based lubricants, because oil-based ones can make condoms break or tear.
PrEP, or pre-exposure prophylaxis, is medicine taken by people without HIV to lower their chance of acquiring it.
It is available free through NHS sexual health services, usually as tablets taken daily or on demand, although some people may need an injection.
PrEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still advised.
PEP, or post-exposure prophylaxis, is a short course of medicine after a possible exposure to HIV.
It is available from sexual health clinics and A&E departments, and the sooner it is started the more likely it is to work.
The CDC advises never sharing needles, syringes or other drug injection equipment.
Terrence Higgins Trust says people living with HIV can now have long, healthy lives.
An NHS sexual health service describes near normal life expectancy with treatment.
HIV services in England are open access, so adults with a diagnosis can refer themselves to a provider of their choice.
Support goes beyond medical care.
Terrence Higgins Trust offers counselling, face to face or online, and a helpline, THT Direct.
It also runs peer support in which everyone taking part is living with HIV, including a group for people recently diagnosed or finding it hard to come to terms with a diagnosis.
Other community organisations listed by an NHS trust include Positive East and Positively UK.
The Trust says one of its aims is to end HIV-related stigma, and its services help people deal with and report hate crime.

An NHS hospital HIV service says most people living with HIV will never develop AIDS, because effective treatment prevents the virus progressing in this way.
Terrence Higgins Trust says someone on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass on HIV.
WHO says a person on antiretroviral treatment who is virally suppressed will not pass HIV to sexual partners.
This is known as U=U, undetectable equals untransmittable.
Condoms still protect against other sexually transmitted infections.
WHO states that casual contact such as kissing or sharing food does not spread HIV.
The NHS says the virus does not spread through the air like cold and flu viruses, and that passing it on through kissing alone is extremely rare.
It is passed on when infected body fluids get into the bloodstream.
There is currently no cure for HIV.
It can be treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from replicating.
With access to effective prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care, WHO describes HIV as a manageable long-term condition that lets people live long and healthy lives.
The NHS provides HIV testing free of charge to anyone, including at sexual health clinics.
Home testing kits and home sampling kits are also available.
If a first test suggests HIV, a further blood test confirms the result.
Early diagnosis means treatment can start sooner.
Also called: Human immunodeficiency virus, HIV infection
What it is: A virus that attacks the immune system
How it is passed on: Through certain body fluids reaching the bloodstream, not through the air or casual contact
Early signs: A short flu-like illness for some people; others have no symptoms for years
Usually diagnosed by: A test at a sexual health clinic or with a home kit, confirmed by a further blood test
Treatment: Daily antiretroviral medicines
Cure: No cure at present; treatment keeps the virus under control
